title: Parent Equals Its Children's Sum
statement:
You get the root of a binary tree that has exactly three nodes: the root, its left child and its right child.

Return true if the root's value equals the sum of its two children's values, and false otherwise.
constraints: The tree has exactly 3 nodes: a root with a left and a right child
hints: The shape is fixed, so there is nothing to traverse. Where do the three values live?
The children are root.left and root.right; neither is null here.

explain.intuition:
This is a warm-up for reading tree nodes. A node is just an object with val, left and right, much like a DOM element with its first and last child. With exactly three nodes guaranteed, both children exist, and the answer is one comparison.

The useful habit here is to notice what the constraints promise. Because the tree always has a left and a right child, no null checks are needed. In the general version, where any node may be missing a child, you would recurse and treat a missing child as contributing 0.
pitfalls: Comparing against only one child, or checking that the children are equal to each other.
Assuming values are positive. [0, -7, 7] is a valid true case.

solutions.title: Direct comparison
solutions.idea: Both children exist, so compare the root with their sum.

followups: Now the tree has any shape. Check that every node with at least one child equals the sum of its children, treating a missing child as 0.
Change as few values as possible so that the rule holds at every node. Where would you start?
